prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence on how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, wage inequality and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred part is still B022 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. I rest the case on research design, scope of consequence and attributable credit, not on the number of members who ranked it. The China-shock papers pose a first-order question: who bears the cost when trade and technology change labour demand, and why adjustment in particular places is slow and costly. They answer it with transparent designs and public data, and the work has been replicated, re-analysed and contested for about a decade. I count that scrutiny in its favour. The contested parts are the size and duration of the effects, and I do not read them as doubt about whether adjustment costs exist. Dorn is a full co-author of the central trade-shock papers, so a three-name set is the faithful attribution for the evidence the citation names. My configuration has not changed on the main points. The chair's round-1 question asks whether the five B022 supporters can agree a single wording. I have narrowed my citation to what is clearly attributable, which is the empirical evidence on technology, import competition, labour demand and local adjustment. It deliberately does not claim the task-based theory, whose originators (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) are outside the credited set. Autor's own work on tasks and polarisation is part of the evidence the citation covers. I would also want the Scientific Background to address the re-analyses of persistence directly. What did change since round 1 is my alternatives: I now list B012 and B007 and have dropped B047, for the reasons given below.
statement.case_against: The credit and scope problem is the main weakness. A citation that mentions technology invites the objection that it under-credits the task framework's other originators. A citation confined to trade shocks leaves out the technology half of the discovery. The magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects are still revised, and shift-share designs face identification critiques. The prize could be read as rewarding a research design and measurement programme more than a conceptual advance. The theme also sits close to the 2024 prize on technology, growth and institutions. I think the 2024 core result, the causal effect of institutions on long-run prosperity, is distinct from the distributional and place-based adjustment findings here, but the Committee could reasonably weigh the proximity as a timing matter. B012 has the longer record of confirmation on firm microdata and a clean two-name attribution. If the Committee prefers a conceptual contribution to trade, B012 is the stronger route.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson now ranks B022 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She drops Katz because his strongest claims are the earlier skill-premium work and the Moving to Opportunity work in B014. Her own citation says 'empirical and conceptual analyses', but she also says the citation should be built around what is clearly attributable, namely the empirical evidence on technology and import competition.
responses.response: I agree on the trio and on leaving Katz out. On wording I would take her second statement over her first. 'Conceptual' invites the Committee to claim the task framework, and its originators lie outside the credited set. That is the one unresolved attribution risk on this ballot. I would use 'empirical evidence' or 'empirical analyses' and keep the theory out of the citation. I also accept her point that the persistence debate concerns the size and duration of the effects, not their direction, and that this belongs in the Scientific Background.

responses.point: Hassler moved to B012 with Melitz and Helpman. He judges firm heterogeneity to have the broader and better-confirmed reach, covering theory, microdata, productivity work and policy evaluation. He also sets aside B021 on attribution grounds.
responses.response: I accept that B012 has the longer and more direct record of confirmation on firm microdata, and I take his own attribution reasoning as sound. Where I differ is on comparability. Breadth of use in trade theory and productivity analysis is one common criterion. Consequence for the understanding of how economies adjust, and for the people and places affected, is another. B022 meets that second criterion more directly. B012's welfare conclusions also depend on functional-form assumptions, as he notes. B022's central findings have been tested in several settings and re-analysed. I do not think the Committee should treat one dimension as decisive. For that reason B012 is my first alternative, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B012 first and names B022 as his first alternative. His reservations about B022 are that the task framework has origins outside the credited set and that the persistence and magnitude of the trade-shock effects are contested. He prefers B012 for its wider footprint across macro, productivity and growth.
responses.response: I share both reservations and have answered them in my citation. It names the empirical evidence, not the task theory. The contest over persistence argues for careful wording, not for waiting. I disagree that the footprint criterion settles the comparison. Evidence that adjustment to trade and technology is slow, local and costly changed how economists and policymakers think about displacement. That is a consequence the B012 framework does not address. I agree with him that Helpman should not appear twice in one award.

responses.point: Krusell keeps B029 first and B047 second. He ranks B022 below B029 on attribution because of the diffuse task credit. He also argues that the 2024 overlap with B047 is merely thematic and that the 2021 prize was a different contribution from the structural methods of B029.
responses.response: His point about diffuse task credit is the one I take most seriously. I accept it for the task framework and have tied the citation to the trade-shock and local-labour-market evidence, where the credit sits with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. His answer on 2024 is why I dropped B047 from my alternatives. I still see the overlap as real adjacent ground, but I also have a field-overlap disclosure on B047 and would rather not argue for it. I said in round 1 that I cannot assess the empirical IO claims, and that remains true. I cannot rank B029 against B022 on its scientific merits. I only note that its attribution depends on a Bresnahan question that its own supporters say is unresolved.

responses.point: Friberg, in his round-1 reply to Teorell, attributes to me a view on Kiyotaki-Moore and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator as two pillars, and a worry about Bernanke's earlier prize.
responses.response: That view is not in my round-1 file, which concerned B022 and its alternatives. I do not want it counted as my position. I have no developed view on the B043 attribution. His case for a two-name B043, and the proximity to 2022, are questions I leave to colleagues with macro-finance expertise.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee can agree a citation that rests on the China-shock and local-labour-market evidence without implicitly claiming the task-model theory whose originators fall outside the credited set.
How far re-analyses and shift-share identification critiques should reduce the weight on the size and persistence of the effects. I cannot settle this from the evidence supplied.

Whether proximity to the 2024 prize should be treated as a reason for delay (a timing judgement) or as a view about the distinctness of the discovery. I think it is distinct, but I cannot show that from the evidence.

Whether B012 and B022 can be compared on common criteria at all. They cover different ground, and I weigh consequence for the adjustment of people and places more heavily than breadth of use in theory and microdata. That weighting is a judgement.
My recollection of credit shares is general knowledge and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for B022 or the alternatives B012 and B007 from the supplied profile. I list no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Helpman, Melitz or Grossman. I withdrew B047 as an alternative. For B047, my profile lists a Governance paper on corruption with 'Persson' and Rothstein, without a first name, so I cannot establish that this is Torsten Persson. My round-1 statement of a co-authorship was stronger than the profile supports, and I do not assert it. My field of comparative political institutions also overlaps closely with B047. I am at Stockholm University, in a different department from committee colleagues Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. My 2024 presentation speech was delivered for the Academy and does not establish a personal voting preference. I disclose these ties and do not adjudicate them.
